title: Evidence-Informed Teaching
author: Paul A. Kirschner
summary: Kirschner adapts Sackett's classic definition of evidence-based medicine to teaching, setting out what evidence-informed teaching is and what it is not. His central argument is that good teaching joins individual teacher expertise with the best available external evidence, and that neither is sufficient alone. He then answers three common objections: that it breeds cook-book teaching, that managers will use it to cut costs, and that it only means randomised trials. The move is a definitional one, using the model of the original medical text to correct misconceptions about research use in classrooms. The piece positions teacher judgment as the arbiter of whether evidence applies to a given student.
points: Evidence-informed teaching integrates teacher expertise with the best available external research, and neither alone is enough.
Expertise without current evidence risks becoming out of date, while evidence without expertise risks being applied inappropriately to an individual student.
It cannot become cook-book teaching because the teacher decides whether and how external evidence applies.
Using it to cut costs misunderstands it, since effective interventions may raise rather than lower the cost of education.
It is not limited to randomised trials and meta-analyses but means tracking down the best evidence for each question.
quotes: Evidence-informed teaching is the conscientious, explicit, and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the education of individual students.
Good teachers use both individual teaching expertise and the best available external evidence, and neither alone is enough.

Without teaching expertise, practice risks becoming tyrannised by evidence, for even excellent external evidence may be inapplicable to or inappropriate for an individual student. Without current best evidence, practice risks becoming rapidly out of date, to the detriment of students.

The practice of evidence-informed teaching is a process of life-long, self-directed learning in which teaching one’s own students creates the need for educationally important information about assessment, learning, instruction, and other educational and teaching issues.

External educational evidence can inform, but can never replace, individual teaching expertise, and it is this expertise that decides whether the external evidence applies to the individual student at all and, if so, how it should be integrated into an educational decision.
Teachers who fear top-down “cook-books” will find the advocates of evidence-informed teaching joining them at the barricades.

Finally, in terms of study designs, evidence-informed teaching is not restricted to randomised trials and meta-analyses. It involves tracking down the best external evidence with which to answer our educational questions.
